title: A reply that depends on the answer
statement: Make every reply depend on what the learner actually said, have each hint add what the answer lacks, and test that every branch, including 'I don't know', can fire.
detail: A research synthesis on the third turn of classroom talk, the reply after a child answers, notes that most instruction and most software stop at a confirmation such as "good", the weakest use of the moment (Shute 2008), and that the clearest sign of a real third turn is a next question that uses what the child just said (Nystrand et al. 1997). Its rule is that a reply that would be the same whatever the child said is not a real response and should be rebuilt. A built Grade 3 lesson applies the idea to choice questions: each wrong option is a coded misconception, and its feedback names that mismatch without quoting the key. A hint must add what the answer lacks, and every branch, including the one for 'I don't know', must be able to fire.
against: A recast, the reply that restates the learner's idea more fully, often goes unnoticed by children and does not reliably teach one specific point, so where something must be learned exactly the same brainlift prefers asking the learner to say it again in their own words (Lyster & Saito 2010, https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263109990520). A later run found counter-evidence (`grade3-reading/incept-read-app/docs/G4-SCR-example-native-qti.md`).

evidence.quote: The clearest sign that the app has taken a real third turn is that its next question uses what the child just said (Nystrand et al., 1997). A reply that would read the same no matter what the child answered is not a third turn.
If the reply would be the same no matter what the child said, it is not a real response and should be rebuilt.
Most instruction, and most software, stops after the child answers and offers only a confirmation such as “good” before moving on, which is the weakest use of the moment (Shute, 2008).
